title: Who Suffers When There is No Self
speaker: John Robinson
summary: The teacher emphasized the importance of direct experience and personal understanding over external authority or dogma, encouraging participants to explore their own experiences with suffering and the concept of self. They noted that our experience of self is often tied to concepts and strategies that can perpetuate suffering, but that by practicing mindfulness and developing skillful habits, we can let go of these patterns and find freedom from angst and confusion. Ultimately, the goal is to cultivate a state of calm contentment, where one feels satisfied with what they have and doesn't desire anything more, leading to discerning choices and relationships that promote happiness and harmony.

Thank you everyone for coming today.
It's a real joy for me to be here.
I love talking about this practice and this teaching and sharing it with others.
It's a joy to see a lot of friends and familiar faces here, and I'm sure I'll get to meet a lot of you later on too.
I can include you in that friendship as well.
Before we get started, I'd like to do a brief guided meditation.
I think it's important, rather than just talking about it, to do it a little bit too, to get a little experience.
So get a comfortable sitting posture.
We're just going to do this for about five minutes.
Close your eyes and take a moment to be here.
You've made the choice to take some time out of this beautiful Saturday morning to come here.
Bring your thoughts into your body.
Be aware of your body just sitting here, listening to my voice, feeling the clothes on your skin and the skin on your body and the body just sitting.
Bring your attention to your heart space, the center of your chest, and take a moment to feel goodwill in that area: kindness, good wishes, the source of bringing happiness to others.
You can begin doing this towards yourself.
Take a moment to maybe visualize yourself in a warm, comfortable area, maybe outside in the sunshine where the temperature is just right, not too cold, not too warm.

May I be happy.
May I be peaceful.
May I be healthy and strong.
May I live with ease and goodwill.
As best as you can, connect with the feeling of goodwill toward yourself.
May I be happy, truly happy.
May I be peaceful and calm.
May I experience health and strength.
May I live with ease and goodwill.
And just bask in that feeling of well-wishing toward yourself.
Then conjure up someone else who can join you in this special place: a friend, someone you care about, someone who's done well for you, friend, relative, benefactor.
Bring them into your circle.
Maybe see a smiling face.
As I wish to be happy, may you be happy.
As I wish to be peaceful and calm, may you be peaceful and calm.
As I wish to be healthy and strong, may you be healthy and strong.
As I wish to live with ease and goodwill, may you live with ease and goodwill.
And then think of someone else, a neutral person.
Someone maybe you see every day but you don't know: a store clerk, someone on the bus, someone you see on the street.
You don't know them.
Bring them into your circle, you and your friend and this neutral person.
May you be happy.
May you be peaceful.
May you experience health and strength.
May you live with ease and goodwill.
Spreading that warmth of goodwill toward your friend, toward this neutral person.
Including others, if you wish, into this.
They just appear.
May you be happy.
May you be peaceful.
May you be healthy.
May you be strong.
May you live with ease and goodwill.
And now invite another person into your circle.
This is someone you may be having difficulty with.
Some unfinished business, maybe some ill will.
Don't take the big ones.
Somewhat simple.
Someone you may have some difficult time with.
Just bring them into the circle of goodwill.
As I wish to be happy, may you be happy.
As I wish to be peaceful, may you be peaceful.
As I wish to be healthy and strong, may you be healthy and strong.
As I wish to live with ease and goodwill, may you too live with ease and goodwill.
May all beings everywhere be happy.
May they be peaceful.
May they be healthy and strong.
May all beings everywhere live with ease and goodwill.
You can open your eyes.
So that's pretty much it.
Actually, the Buddha taught 50 or so different meditations, and this was just one kind.
It's called loving kindness or goodwill meditation, also known as Metta, which is a Pali word for loving kindness.
It's one aspect of Metta meditation.

I just wanted to introduce that to you, because I think often when we feel a little scattered and unhappy, and maybe a little irritable, this is a place that we can always come to, a place of calm and peace.
It's actually your capacity to do that at any time.
I wanted to tell you a little bit about what I'm going to talk about this morning.
I've been practicing this practice for about 32 years.
I'm kind of a slow learner, so it's good that we have this opportunity to keep practicing.
This tradition is called the Theravada tradition, and the meditation practice is called Vipassana.
That's one type of meditation.
The one we did this morning was Metta, but the larger meditation is called Vipassana.
The Theravada practice of the Buddhist lineage is, I call it, kind of the orthodox.
This was the teaching that seemed to have come out of India three or four or five hundred years after the death of the Buddha, twenty-five hundred years ago, and got written down.
Currently this practice is pretty embedded in Southeast Asia: Thailand, Burma, Sri Lanka, Laos, Cambodia, a little bit of Vietnam.
And now in the West, in Europe too.
So it has a lot of reference back to some of the original teachings, or the original words of the Buddha.
Theravada means the teachings of the elders, so it really comes from a monastic perspective of the teachings.
Then the monastics, or the elders, share this with the lay community.
So it has an interesting culture, I think, of people who do this intense practice, sort of away from the trappings of the world.
Monks don't handle money and they don't drive cars and they have 227 different rules they have to abide by.
It's a very strong community, and with that intense practice they are able to share their wisdom with the lay community.
Now, just in the last 60 or so years, lay teachers of this practice are out and about.
I would consider myself one of those lay teachers who are very much involved in the world and also practice these Theravadan teachings.
That's the perspective.
What I want to talk about today is some of the challenges or issues that we get to practice with, because this teaching really is something you have to experience yourself directly.
There's a term, the Dharma.
Oftentimes the word Dharma is translated as the teachings of the Buddha, and I think it's a little more than that.
I think the Buddha was actually teaching what is already out there, which is the truth.
A lot of the time what the Buddha was talking about was pointing to the truth, or the Dharma.
One of the big things he was saying was that you have to go and experience it yourself.
Don't believe this just because I say it's true or someone else says it's true.
Don't believe it just because it's written down in some sacred text or because someone told you this was a good thing to go and do.
Don't even believe in me, but go and experience this for yourself.
If you find that it's beneficial, that it brings benefit to your life and it's blameless, then continue the practice.
But if you find that it doesn't provide benefit in your life, and peace and happiness, then let it go and seek elsewhere.
That's what brought me to this practice: okay, it puts the responsibility onto me.
There's not going to be some savior out there.
Or if I just take the one, two, three steps of Buddhist practice or whatever practice, then I'll be somehow permanently happy.
But I have to actually walk the path and walk the steps, experiencing the experiences as they come up.
So it's a very personal process that we need to do.
One of the real founding principles, I guess, or concepts of Buddhism is called the Four Noble Truths.
These Four Noble Truths have many layers and many levels to them.
I'll just introduce the concept, because I know some of you are probably very familiar with them.
Some of you may have read about them but don't know what that all means.
The Buddha said that the First Noble Truth is that there is suffering in the world.
He called it dukkha, and dukkha is a Pali word that has many different translations.
Suffering is one of them.
Another translation is that there's stress, that there's dissatisfaction in the world, that we have a little angst in our lives.
It may be very subtle, it may be very profound, but there's an angst that we live with.
And there's a cause that causes that angst in our world, in our existence.
What causes that angst is craving, or clinging to what we want and pushing away what we don't want.
The Third Noble Truth is that there is a way out of that trap, out of that dilemma that we're constantly living and reliving and reliving.
And that's the Fourth Noble Truth, which is the Eightfold Noble Path.
I won't go into the Eightfold Noble Path in a lot of detail today.
I'll strip it down to three basic categories: virtue, or conscious conduct; concentration and contentment; and discernment, or wisdom practice.
When I first started doing this practice, maybe the first ten years, I got this idea of the Four Noble Truths: okay, I crave things and I hold on to things or I want things to be a certain way.
When things aren't a certain way, then I'm unhappy, when they don't unfold exactly as I want to control them.
We're always trying to control our world or our universe, and then when things don't happen exactly the way they are, we're unhappy with that.
So I said, okay, I'll open up to the idea that maybe I don't need to be in control.
And so what do I crave?
What are the things I hold on to?
Well, I hold on to sense objects: pleasant sounds, pleasant tastes, pleasant sensations.
I hold on to pleasant ideas, that this idea is the right way to go and the right way to do, and so I'm going to practice this and do this.
If it changes, then it better not change, because I'm really going to hold on to this and it's got to stay the same.
So there's a real struggle there, right?
So I thought, well, all I needed to do was let go of all of these objects out there that I hold on to, my favorite sensations, my favorite foods.
So I spent a lot of time renouncing these kinds of things.
It became pretty clear pretty quickly that I was missing the point, that there wasn't a certain quality of discernment in this plan, that it wasn't the objects that were creating my suffering.
They're just being objects.
They're being new clothes, interesting people, nice food.
They're just doing their thing.
It was my action of clinging to them and wanting them to stay with me or, if it was unpleasant, to push it away.
So I said, okay, then the next level must be that I need to let go of grasping, just quick.
This will see when I grasp and then let go and be soft about it.
So I looked at the verb: when am I leaning towards something and wanting to keep things the way they are?

I worked with that for a few years, saying, okay, I caught the times when I really was leaning forward or I was really avoiding something I didn't like, pushing away and going, it shouldn't be that way, or life should be fair, those kinds of things.
So, okay, look at that and go, okay, let go of that idea.
Well, it still didn't seem quite right.
It still wasn't the whole picture.
Probably after about 10 or 12 years of my practice, I finally got it that the attachment wasn't the attachment or the clinging to sense objects, or so much the verb of doing that.
So it's important to be aware of when you get caught in things.
It was my attachment to the concept of I or me or mine which was the hardest one to let go of.
I mean, when you come face to face with that, it was like, oh, wait a minute.
It's like one big rug got pulled out from underneath me.
Oh, it's this I, like I've got to do the practice or I've got to let go or I've got to have a different relationship or whatever it may be.
It was the I that was keeping me suffering or unhappy, that angst.
So what do I mean by that sort of self?
The title of this talk is If There's No Self, Who Suffers?
It's a little bit of an oxymoron.
So that's what we're headed towards here.
I wanted to define what suffering is.
Let's talk a little bit about what self is.
Now, oftentimes it's written that the Buddha said there was no self.
The interesting thing is, if you go into the text, as they've been written and recorded through the centuries, the Buddha didn't really say there was no self.
And he didn't really say that there was a self either.
So which one is it?
Is there a self?
Is there not a self?
Is there no self?
So there was a little bit of a dilemma.
The way the Buddha answered questions, he answered questions as a teaching tool.
He usually answered questions in four ways.
He either answered them directly, which is for a very simple question.
Is this a skillful act or is this not a skillful act?
He would answer that fairly directly, for example.
Or maybe the question that was asked would need some clarification, and they would have to expound on that a little bit.
Or sometimes someone would ask a question and then it would be a counter question, sort of turn it back onto the questioner.
And then there's the fourth kind of question, the one he advised people to set aside.
Is there a self?
Is there not a self?
It's one of those fourth types of questions.

His choice in doing that, I think, was because speculating whether there's a self or not a self can create a lot more confusion, and that speculation can create a lot of misconceptions and get lost in that.
He always wanted to avoid those kinds of questions, like is there a God?
Is there not a God?
Is there eternalism?
Is there not eternalism?
He would say these kinds of questions, even if we could answer them, would not assist us in our journey to being free from suffering.
So he would lay them aside and say this is not what I teach.
This is not important.
Which was a big struggle back in those days because there were a lot of different teachers around, a lot of different philosophies, a lot of different practices going on in India at the time.
But he said [unclear: "fast"], this is not one that we should spend a lot of time contemplating, the self, no self.
So I wanted to delve into that a little bit so we can get a little clarification.
If I ask you if there's a self, how do you experience it?
We probably all could go into some idea about how we experience self: I have a name, I have an identity, I have roles, I have relationships, people call me by my name, those kinds of things.
So we have a self in that sense, a conventional self.
In that sense there's a self.
If you look at it a little bit deeper, what do we experience?
Where is the self in the body?
If you just close your eyes right now and go, okay, where is the self?
How do I experience the self?
Is it my body?
Is it my heart?
Is it my mind?
How do I directly experience self?
Is it a thought?
But that thought's changed and left, so now I don't have a self anymore.
So where is the self?
Well, there isn't a self in the sense that there's some lasting, holding, permanent, physical self that we know of.
But we operate as if there is.
One teacher recently talked about how the self is a strategy.
It's a moving, changing kind of thing.
And another way of looking at the self is as a concept.
Now, concepts are ideas about something else.
So we walk around talking about the self, and let me give you an example.
This is a classic example and I always like to share this.
I pardon those who've heard this story 16 times.

An example of a concept, especially the concept of self, is this: if you look outside at night and you see the stars, and it's a little bit difficult these days because we have a beautiful full moon and a clear sky, but when the moon's not so strong, you can look up in the sky and you can see the stars, little points of light.
That's the direct experience, points of light.
And there are certain patterns of points of light, and one of those patterns is the Big Dipper.
There are five, six stars that make up the Big Dipper, points of light.
We all pretty much know we can find the Big Dipper in the sky when the stars are out.
Now if you could somehow change the channel in your viewing and not see that pattern anymore, and see, oh, how do you not see the Big Dipper?
But we all know there's not a Big Dipper up there.
We know there's not some big tin dipper up there that holds the heavens, but it's really hard to not see the concept of Big Dipper.
And that's what we've got to challenge around the concept of self.
We live it, we embody that idea, that concept of self, all the time in our conventional daily life.
And it's important because if we didn't, we'd be sleeping in a different house every night, because we wouldn't know whose house is whose.
It'd be a real problem.
We all have keys, but we wouldn't know which cars they went into because it's like, who are you?
So it's important that we can function on that level.
The problem becomes when we begin to believe the concept to be the reality.
That's where the problem comes, when we start living our lives as if self is something real.
I'm going to give you an example.
Well, we probably all have examples, but there's a time when you have to build up the self to impress others, for example, or we're worried about what people will think of us.
How many of us have that little voice in the mind?
It's the commentator.
What would people think if I did this?
Or what would people think if I think this?
It goes on and on and on and on and on.
Worry, worry, worry, worry.
It's like your school records.
If you remember in grade school, you've got to do good or it'll be in your records, right?
And then you won't get to the next step.
Like there's some scorekeeper in the sky or somewhere.
That's what I mean about the struggle of thinking that the self is real.
And we lose the perspective of how we make a practice out of this.
So we have the conventional self, and then we have the ultimate self.
The ultimate self, there is no self.
And where suffering happens, or when this angst happens, is when we're caught in this idea of self and try to live out this image of something being real when it's illusionary.
So on one level, we have to live this illusion so that we can have a bed to sleep in at night and we can have relationships and we can carry on our lives.
And on the other level, it doesn't really matter.
It's a real perplexing situation.
It's like, I thought this was supposed to be easy.
I thought it was supposed to be an easy practice.
So there's a little bit of confusion here, or could be confusion here.
But I want to point out that what we're trying to look at in this practice is moving from unskillful habits and unskillful points of view to skillful habits and skillful points of view.
Once we realize that, okay, self isn't something real and permanent and physical, that it's a convention that we all operate in and it has a certain value to a point, and then it's not useful.
It's like your old computers.
When you got your new computer, it was really useful.
It was fast and you got all these kinds of things.
But then all of a sudden, in two or three years, well, for me it's two or three years, for most people it's six months, all of a sudden the new programs don't fit anymore and it's useless.
So at some point that conventional view of self doesn't help us to that state of freedom from that angst and freedom from that confusion that we may experience.
So how do we work with this paradox?
And it's a practice.
You hear this a lot from all of the people that come up here and speak in the next few weeks: practice.

What we're trying to do is move from a place of untrained reaction to things, of grasping things as if this is going to make me happy and make myself more real, to a place of looking at how that creates confusion.
I'm just going to give you a couple of ideas to work with.
The Eightfold Path, and I don't like to use the word path, but that's how it's translated.
I think of it as more of a tree or maybe even a helix.
You know what a DNA strand looks like?
That's a double helix, two strands that swirl around.
Well, think of it as eight strands that co-mingle and coexist with each other.
That's your project, that's the life project.
I'll break them down into three categories: conscious conduct or virtue, concentration and contentment, and the third is wisdom or discernment.
Conscious conduct is usually translated as virtue, but I think some of us may have a bit of an angst around, you know, what I should do and shouldn't do.
This is the good and bad of your life, like what are the good things, what are the skillful things to do, what are the unskillful things to do?

In my particular practice we talk about the five precepts, and the five precepts are non-killing, non-stealing, non-lying, refraining from sexual misconduct, and not taking intoxicants that cloud the mind.
For lay people that's a pretty good covering.
These are not commandments, these are not thou shalt not kill or thou shalt not lie.
These are practices.
What's it feel like?
How does it create joy or ill will in your mind when you kill, for example, or what is skillful speech?
I like to frame it, rather than being non-killing, non-harming, those kinds of things, as looking at what harmlessness is in your life.
How does that help you?
How does that create joy in your life, or how does that work for you?
How does generosity, how does giving and caring and helping out, how does that fit into your life?
How does that work for you?
Is that something that's painful?
Is that something that's easy, that's joyful?
And so forth and so on.
How about skillful speech?
The times when speech creates harmony and connection and provides information for people, and when is it disharmonious, those kinds of things.
Those are the practices, okay.
How to do relationships that create love and connection and respect.
And the last one, not taking intoxicants that cloud the mind: how about the kinds of refraining or renunciation of those things that will actually expound on your investigation and your curiosity?
Is watching a lot of television an intoxicant?
Or is that something skillful that creates more wisdom?
Is moderation of foods and drink and so forth helpful, or is that a difficulty for you?
These are practices that you ask yourself as you do these things.
Those are the five precepts around virtue.
It's a lifetime practice right there, and you could stop right there and be in depths and depths and depths of wisdom just paying attention to those practices.
The concentration part of the Eightfold Path is broken down into right effort, right concentration, and right mindfulness.
I like to simplify that, and if you look at the spaces in your life, maybe the next time you want to go purchase something, feel what it feels like to want something, and at what point do you own it?
Is it when you put that item in your basket?
Is it when you pay for it and you're walking out the door?
Or is it when you open up the package?
Or is it when you plug it in?
When is it mine?
The other part of that practice is when do you feel content?
Ah!
Which sounds, from the audience, like a little bit of an illusion.
I'll be happy for a minute.
But there's a place in wanting and not wanting things to happen where there's a balance, where there's a kind of contentment.
When the Buddha was reflecting on his enlightenment, he remembered a time when he was an adolescent.
The Buddha, before his enlightenment, was a prince, and he had all the worldly things he ever wanted.
When he was a teenager, he was at a festival.
He was the champion rider on the horses, and he was the champion this and champion that.
He was just really successful.
Of course, this is a legend, so everything went right for the Buddha.
He was taking a break from the festival, and he was sitting under a rose apple tree, which is not something around here, it's actually a tropical tree.
But he experienced this contentment of not having any lack and not wanting anything.
And he remembered that back at the time when he was enlightened.
He said, that is an important mind state to cultivate, a place of just, it's enough.
There's nothing lacking.
So investigating that place of calm and contentment is a really important practice.
In that place of calm and contentment, then we can see what's useful in our lives and what's not so useful in our lives.
That's the discernment part of this practice.
Then we can begin to look at, oh, okay, I guess I didn't really need to have three of those.
One was enough.
Okay, that feels okay.
And now I don't have to worry about harboring the other two.
We begin to make skillful choices and skillful relationships when we're able to see, in a state of contentment, what's beneficial and what's skillful.
And all of this is actually in relation, I didn't have enough time to talk about this, but in relationship to how we are interacting with everyone else.

That's why I started this talk with the loving kindness meditation, that it doesn't happen in the sense of me and mine, but it happens in the sense of being boundless in your goodwill towards yourself and others.

So this practice is very much involved with everyone, every being, and when you can see that the generosity and the kindness and the skillfulness that you do is in relationship with everyone else, then we begin to open up to that contentment and happiness.
So it's not a self or not self, it's also that there's an us, us, us, us in all of this.
And it's important to see how our choices and our actions and our thoughts promote that happiness or create more discord.
